title: Wayseeking Mind
speaker: Joden Bob Rose
summary: Joden Bob Rose tells the story of how a life arrives at steady Zen practice, framed by a Lou Welch poem and Dogen's chapter on the Bodhisattva's Four Methods of Guidance. Joden traces the path from a Miami childhood and pre-med studies at Tufts through poetry in Buffalo, boatbuilding in Vancouver, and decades of land conservation in the Skagit Valley and Hawaii. A shipyard teaches giving as Dogen describes it. A Lonely Planet listing for Saturday tours at San Francisco Zen Center leads to a week's residency, a chair offered for aching knees, and Blanche Hartman's advice to visit the Bellingham sangha. Joden closes with the Tenzo's prayer offered to Nomon Tim when he became the sangha's guiding teacher.

sentences.text: *An unsurpassed, penetrating, and perfect dharma is rarely met with even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
Good morning, good friends and fellow bodhisattvas.
This morning, I'd like to speak to you about coming to continuous practice.
I'd like to begin with a couple of quotes to recognize where we are and where I am.
The first is from a great American poet, Ezra Pound, who brought Chinese poetry to our language early in the last century.

Late in his life, he wrote, *It all coheres, all right, even if my notes do not cohere.* And a poem by Lou Welch, who, with Gary Snyder and Philip Whalen, met at Reed College, and they really brought Buddhism forth in American poetry in a great burst that we all benefit from now.
Lou Welch wrote this poem, which I came across in 1969, called "A Small Sentence to Drive Yourself Sane."

*The next time you are doing something absolutely ordinary, or even better, the next time you are doing something absolutely necessary, such as pissing or making love or shaving or washing the dishes or the baby or yourself or the room, say to yourself, so it's all come to this.*
Today is the version of a story of my life and how I've come to a pretty steady and continuous practice for the past 10 years, with roots that run deep in ways that I can't begin to fathom.
I came to formal practice late in life, at age 65, but encountered Dharma early, in 1967, at the age of 22.
As the Vietnam horror accelerated, I stumbled on the edicts of Ashoka, the great patron of Buddhism in third century BC India, while I was preparing my conscientious objector application.
That book is still in my library, and I came across a reference to Ashoka in an essay of Dogen's.
I opened up my book and found underlined in there, *establish the community of mankind on the basis of Dharma, respect each other and perform good deeds.*
Forty-five years later, a pivotal life moment grabbed my shoulder.
In March of 2010, my companion and I were in San Francisco on a home exchange, and we carried our faithful Lonely Planet guidebook.
I opened it up and it said, if you're interested, check out Saturday morning tours at the San Francisco Zen Center.
So I took the trolley up Market Street and stayed for tea.

Standing in the courtyard in conversation with the gray-robed female monk Joan Amaral, who is now the founder of the North Shore Zen Center in Massachusetts, I told her about my carpentry and farming history, and she said, "Why don't you come to Tassajara?"
That brought me up short, but there had been some recent preparation.
The year before, I had purchased a Nepalese singing bowl from my son's Barcelona Fairtrade import store.
When I came home, I read a book about their use in history.
That led me to opening a book I had on my bookshelf for many years called *The Teachings of the Buddha*, which is actually the Gideon's Bible of Asia, found in any hotel room in the drawer.
I soon realized the key to Buddhist teachings was meditation.
So I began sitting occasionally during the summer of 2009, and a few months later, I was in the City Center courtyard.
Intrigued by the idea of Zen in Tassajara, in early June 2010, I applied for and was accepted for an informal week-long residency at City Center.
My bed was in a plywood cubby in the basement.
The giant han sounded down the hall at the foot of the stairs.

The first morning, walking into the zendo, I felt like I had come home, but I was discouraged by my aching knees. [unclear: "Tonto"] Jordan Thorne, rest in peace, counseled me, "You know, you can sit in a chair like Maitreya."
And thus began a practice of regular sitting, after spending a life resistant to imposed structure, direction and ritual.
And most surprising, I kept coming back over and over.
What causes and conditions brought me to that moment, and the practice life that has unfolded since and is unfolding in this moment?
I will try to tell that story as best I can today.
In a recent Zen talk, Zoketsu Norman Fischer offered this: "The given of our lives is where and when you are born and your parents.
From there forward, we are the master of our lives.
We make choices.
This reality is the best reality, the only reality we could have.
Each of our lives is an expression of Dharma.
No lives, no Dharma."
It seems like we are born, we leave home and, if fortunate, find our way back to Buddha.

So let's go back, bring it forward to the apparent moment of my entering this vast and wide world, and follow today's version of a trail that winds from South Florida to Northwest Washington, the long diagonal.
It's been a life full of surprises, deep friendships, good health and good fortune.
Born in Boston as World War II ended, raised by two loving parents with modest incomes of teacher and accountant.
Never a raised voice in anger, but with firm discipline.
A drama-free life of stability and a welcoming home for friends, with delicious homemade food, lots of books and great love of classical music and jazz.
At age five, we moved to Coral Gables, Florida, where I grew up in a reformed Jewish tradition.
Bar Mitzvah and confirmed, but no spirit, no focus on spirituality.

Although interestingly enough, just last month my brother told me, after being ordained as a rabbi in Jerusalem, that I had inspired him to this path, because as he listened to me practicing my chants for my bar mitzvah, he said, "I want to do that."
And here he is now, an orthodox rabbi at age 72.
I was a nerdy young scientist working in laboratories during the four summers in high school, and I was focused on a career as a doctor.
But I did take wood shop.
"What are you doing with all those greasers?" asked my best friend, who went on to become the head of surgery at Harvard.
That eighth grade class opened astonishing Dharma gates.
Miami was then the segregated South.
I remember purposefully drinking from the colored water fountain at the municipal bus station.
My dad befriended and did bookkeeping for Mr.
Anderson, a black nursing home owner.
But I was repelled by the materialistic culture of South Florida.
I left the day after graduating high school for a summer job in Maine and the pre-med program at Tufts University in Boston, right on a straight course.
First year pre-med was easy because I went to a great high school, but I was always a party lover.
Year two, things started going sideways.

The combination of Saturday morning organic chemistry classes, finding out about weed, and realizing I didn't really like my fellow pre-med students, I changed to be an English major and got involved in the literary magazine and the pre-hippie cool crowd.
It was a time of transition from civil rights protests to the Vietnam War heating up.
Grad school looked like the way to avoid the draft.

Senior year, I happened to take a contemporary American poetry class that opened my eyes and ears, discovering Gary Snyder, the Beats, and Charles Olson, all in a radical, non-academic anthology called The New American Poetry.
By chance, grad school in Buffalo brought me in immediate contact with some of those same poets in real life, and they developed lifelong friendships and a camaraderie.
Charles Olson's poetics, Robert Creeley's friendship, Robert Duncan's incredible mind opened vast imaginative landscapes.
Gary Snyder's work inspired West Coast dreams.
Over the next decades, I hung out with, published, and studied with some of America's revolutionary poets.
Great companions, as my subsequent teacher in Vancouver, Robin Blazer, would call this [unclear: "fire source group"].
It was at Buffalo I first heard about the 1965 Berkeley Poetry Conference, where those poets read and expounded a new vision of language in the public world.
We listened, glued to precious, fuzzy, fourth-generation, [unclear: "wall-and-sack"], reel-to-reel recordings, hanging on every word.
And it turns out the whole week-long event was organized by a Berkeley faculty member named Richard Baker.
Forty years later, I realized it was the same person who secured City Center, Green Gulch, Tassajara, and subsequent events, as told in Shoes by the Door.
I learned poetry deeply and grew with mantra-like passages of Olson's that I now realize deeply resonate with our Zen teachings.
Let me share a few of them with you.
One of his favorites was from the pre-Socratic philosopher Heraclitus, a near contemporary of Buddha:
*Man estranged from that with which he is most familiar.*
*We do what we know before we know what we do.
I am one with my skin.
I am naked, the man said, and nakedness is what one means, that all start up to the eye and soul as though it had never happened before.*
And probably my favorite: oh poet, you should get a job.
Another touchstone came from Allen Ginsberg, "Who Be Kind To," where he opens by saying:
*Who be kind to?
Be kind to yourself.
It is only one and perishable of many on the planet.
Thou art that one.*
One day over beers, after a reading in New York City, Creeley looked at me and said, "I see you."
And I truly felt genuine and understood for the first time.
Maybe it was at that reading where he also spoke the Dogen-like line, "The first person you meet when you walk into a room is yourself."

After a year of grad school, recognizing a Ph.D. was not in my cards, I left with a master's degree and landed a teaching job at a podunk state college in Bridgewater, Massachusetts, 40 miles south of Boston, commuting from Cambridge.
The summer of 1969, I visited a friend in the Navy on Whidbey Island and was offered a job the next summer building houses.
I returned east, wrote a letter of resignation for the year's end, and headed west in June of 1970.
I now realize this was my moment of home leaving.

A middle class Jewish kid from Miami drives west to Whidbey Island, encounters wilderness, divests from the cultural expectations of a very conventional upbringing, and follows the idea of Gary Snyder's lead until I realized that setting choker wasn't probably such a good idea.
So building houses seemed a little safer.
I spent the summer of 1970 hiking and climbing in the North Cascades and never looked back.
I've been living within 60 miles of where I landed ever since.
I had found my new home, the Skagit world that Jack Kerouac described in Dharma Bums on his way up to [unclear: "Sourgo Mountain"] as:
*Rich, butterfat valleys with farms and cows browsing under that tremendous background of snow-pure heaps.*
Only later did I realize that Jack, Snyder, Whalen, and a whole sangha of poets and painters, Fishtown poets and painters, also made the beloved Magic Skagit home.

That was the beginning of a most fortunate sequence of 12-year, more or less, careers of right livelihood, working as a carpenter, shipwright, and in land conservation as advocate, government official, nonprofit director, and consultant.
All work that in great measure I loved doing and in which I never felt I was just biding my time or causing harm.
After framing custom houses on Whidbey Island for a couple of years, my girlfriend left and headed for Astoria.
During a moment of bereft loneliness on the beach at [unclear: "Snakelin Point"], I realized: the joke is on you.
Only you care.
So what?
Might as well take a deep breath, remember to laugh at yourself, and keep going.
So I left for Vancouver a few months later to join the cadre of poets I had become familiar with via some of my Buffalo connections.
The first job fell through and I got the wild-hair idea of learning how to build wooden boats, and began a life period of shipyards and poetry.

Apprenticing at Wall Shipyards and Northarm Boatworks, I began to understand what Ishmael in Moby Dick meant when he says, *"The whale ship was my Yale College and my Harvard."* My mom and dad visiting me from Miami weren't so sure.
Their pre-med Ivy League-educated college professor son had turned into a long-haired, overall-wearing, calloused-hand tradesman building 60-foot wooden fishing boats.
Oy vey!
But, unbeknownst to me, I was learning a core lesson about giving and generosity.
In Chapter 46 of the Shobogenzo, the Bodhisattva's Four Methods of Guidance, Dogen tells us:
*To launch a boat or build a bridge is an act of giving.
Making a living and producing things can be nothing other than giving.
Great King Ashoka, everything comes around, was able to offer enough food for hundreds of monks with half a [unclear: "mirrobalan"],* that's a small plum fruit.
*People who practice giving should understand that King Ashoka thus proved the greatness of giving.*
Or as my carpenter poet friend David Phillips wrote:
*At the shipyard, I discovered the deep satisfaction of hands, sharp tools, and wood, far beyond previous work as a simple nail-pounder.

Working Doug fir and yellow cedar timbers, using saw, chisel, and mallet to fit beam-end tenons into tight mortise pockets in a stringer, you embody the fitting of wood to wood, knowing this is not a mere exercise in craft, but an essential joint in building a wooden boat.
Not a trinket or an item of luxury, but of necessity.
Far more than simple beauty, though it is that too, it is a working vessel to provide sustenance and a livelihood for its owners and a crew, whose lives depend on your attention and workmanship.
The sharpness of your tools and the accuracy of your cut lines define the outcome.
No wobble, no play.*
*This is the real world, where good enough must be good and enough, no more, no less.
Here, box and lid fit, for real.*
Each and every piece of the Dharma world, the net of Indra, is perfection on its own.
All pieces belong as they are, where they are.
A well-joined vessel does not leak.
At age 30, I took a break from the shipyard and left North America for the first time, and entered the vast and wide world of Latin America for the necessary [unclear: "coming-of-the-mill"].
As a sole traveler with little money, doling out pennies for cigarettes, I experienced real loneliness, discovered self-sufficiency for the first time, and learned to trust the journey.
Continual bouts of amoebic dysentery over four months of travel taught me a special kind of humility and patience with my body.
At points in that journey, I made vows that I have lived with since, to live with no regrets.
I took to heart the words of Black Pitcher Satchel Page, who I watched play for the AAA Miami League Mariners: "Don't look back.
Something might be gaining on you."
To make choices each moment as if it was the last, and to face fully what I was doing in that moment.
And to listen to my gut instinct, the strength I've learned to trust, a trait I received from my mother Gladys.

Dysentery emaciated, I came back to live a hermit-like life, caretaking a friend's property on Hornby Island, where I met the island doctor, my wife-to-be for the next 24 years, with her then five-year-old daughter.
Rachel, just turned 50, was Vancouver's poet laureate and is an internationally acclaimed writer.
Our son, Jefferson, is an accomplished world music bass player whose band helped [unclear: "Noamon Tim"] celebrate his 50th birthday.
There is a great harmony and love among the three of us.
They are the joy of my life.
In 1976, we moved back to the Skagit, buying a small house on the side of Mount Erie.
As an American poet, Canada had become politically hostile, and there was lots of boat work in Anacortes, a then-thriving fishing town.
The next year, the writer's gathering at Centrum Port Townsend opened the door to sitting with Zenshin Philip Whelan every morning for a week and then driving him to Seattle.

Gary Snyder was there as well, and I met Sam Hamill, rest in peace, Tim McNulty, Michael Daly, longtime publisher of Empty Bowl Press and of many Red Pine texts, the gang of Port Townsend poets and tree planters, all Dharma pals to this day, defining bioregionalism and re-inhabiting planet Earth.
And every Solstice week for the many years, we have now gathered at [unclear: "Chi Chi"] on the Olympic Coast for a Wilderness Coast Session together.
That's why I haven't been at Samish very much.
Pretty soon after that, the local newspaper reported that the State Department of Natural Resources planned to lease Heart Lake for condominiums and clear-cut 160 acres visible from Deception Pass.
Heart Lake is surrounded by old-growth forests at the base of Mount Erie, just outside of Anacortes.
I went to a neighborhood meeting and it was like opening a door and falling down an elevator shaft.
Suddenly I was in the news as lead spokesperson and in Olympia working to pass legislation to protect this 400-acre pristine ecosystem.
Years later, we found out that Heart Lake is the best remaining Douglas fir cedar hemlock forest at sea level left in the state.

And it was the keystone in the 3,000-acre corridor of city-owned land with largely intact old-growth and recovering second-growth forests, the old watershed lands of the city, stretching from the San Juan Ferry terminal to Deception Pass Park.
There was no plan for its future.
I raised the need to city council, and before I knew it, I was in charge of chairing the committee and writing the Anacortes Community Forest Lands Plan.
"You should do this professionally," I was told by a state park planner, and I took his advice seriously.
Having challenged the DNR, I signed up to work on the 1980 State Land Commissioner Campaign to successfully oust the 24-year incumbent Old King Bert Cole.
And to finance my way back to graduate school at the University of Washington, I worked the summer of 1981 on a 42-foot fishing vessel, the Desperado, a boat I had rebuilt the year before.
We motored north and fished Kodiak Island.
I was cook and deckhand.
Perfect tenzo training.
Four men in a very tight space, a floating hermitage.
And the best part of being cook was avoiding standing thigh-high in the fish hold, pitching off salmon at midnight to the tender.
Back to school at UW, I landed an internship with the new DNR.
The Anacortes experience was seen by the commissioner as a model of community-based resource planning.
So my assignment was to put together the plan for the Tiger Mountain State Forest just outside of Issaquah.

And over the next 10 years as a special assistant to the commissioner, my assignments included protecting all the DNR lands in the San Juan Islands, and then I drafted, lobbied, and helped implement the Natural Resource Conservation Areas Law that protects outstanding examples of [unclear: "NATO"] ecosystems, habitat for endangered, threatened, and sensitive plants and animals, and scenic landscapes.

Today, there's 125,000 acres and 39 NRCAs protected in the state, including 95% of Cypress Island, a huge amount of [unclear: "Mount Sy"], and near Bellingham, the south end of Lummi Island, the Lake Louise Preserve, this part of the Stimson Reserve, that are now permanently safeguarded.
The poet Shelley said famously, "Poets are the unacknowledged legislators of the world."
But I realized one night that here was a case where legislators were the unacknowledged poets of the world.
Sadly and unexpectedly, my mom died in 1992 just at the end of my DNR tenure, and I was about to go to work for the Nature Conservancy.
But instead, we bought a four-acre Skagit Valley farm three miles east of La Conner on some of the best soil in the world.
My wife grew Northwest native bulbs, and I focused on small-scale market farming for local restaurants and the Anacortes Farmers Market.
Local farm leader Dave Headland asked me to join the board of Skagitonians to preserve farmland.
Within a year, I became the one-day-a-week executive director.
Then over the next 12 years, it grew to a full-time job with staff.
And early on, we came up with the bumper sticker, which you've probably seen: "Protect Skagit farmland.
Pavement is forever."
By the time I left in 2006, there were about 60,000 of those out.
I'm not sure how many are out there now.
But that was part of a campaign to get our county commissioners to pass a conservation futures farmland legacy program.
And now 25 years later, this farmer-supported program permanently protects 12,000 acres on over 200 farms in the Skagit Valley.
We also work to ensure the future of the WSU research station by protecting the surrounding lands.
And that inspired WSU to invest $8 million in this worn-out facility to serve all of Western Washington farming.

Well, stepping down from SPF at the end of 2006, various consulting jobs and rebuilding two historic barns at my dear friend David Headland's farms were punctuated by a series of home exchanges with Mary Lynn, my steady partner over the past 18 years.
We went everywhere from Australia to Amsterdam and took trips to Peru, Costa Rica, and Venice.
One morning in Venice, [unclear: "arrow points met"].
I'd like to read you a little poem.
It's called "Meeting John Wiley in Venice on Calle de la Pieta Bridge."
*In the morning, we retraced our steps to find our misplaced backpack left in our hurry to hear Vivaldi's Four Seasons performed in his own Chiesa de Santa Maria de la Pieta.
Rare as an ancient tortoise surfacing every hundred years for a deep breath in the middle of an oxen's yoke floating in the vast ocean, [unclear: "amigo de Beleham and Kyoto"].*

During the past decade of deepening Zen practice, a Dharma gate opened to a project in Hawaii where I now work with the Hawaiian Island Land Trust, Kamehameha Schools, the largest landowner in the state, and Taylor Guitars to restore and establish endangered native koa forests.
In Hawaii, land is *aina*.
Learned elders and practitioners of native culture have taught me their ethic: we take care of the land and the land takes care of us.
But it is not land without people.
It is a reciprocal relationship.
Just as there is no Dharma without our lives, there is no land without people.
These descendants of the greatest navigating culture the world has known also have a saying profoundly relevant to our current condition.
The canoe is an island, the island is a canoe.
Island Earth is our canoe, and our responsibility is to take care of all its beings.
Over these past three decades, causes and conditions brought me to these situations as an apparent leader.
But I was only the point of an arrow, supported and fashioned by so many others.
In my role at DNR, SPF, and in Hawaii, I have been an agent, the tool for something so much larger.
There's a saying in the land trust community that the land speaks for itself.

And I have joyously had the opportunity and responsibility to hear that voice and to be one of the canoe's tools for helping to save all beings by protecting ecosystems at whatever scale the opportunity provided.
It's been a small start and there is so much more to do.

In one of his recent talks on the springing up from the Earth chapter of the Lotus Sutra, Zoketsu offered that the natural world is a message from an image of and a voice of the ultimate realm, the realm beyond our historical realm.
At a publication celebration, my son and I attended *Four Poets on the Peaks*, a book portraying the beat's lookout time in the North Cascades.
Gary Snyder said, "Wilderness gives us a brief contact with eternity in action."
Each time I walk in the Heart Lake old growth and sit on my favorite log with a cup of tea, I venerate my abiding companions.
We bow to each other with great affection.
In his Lotus Sutra commentary, Thich Nhat Hanh points us to a figure called Earth Holder Bodhisattva, Dhranindhara, whose name means to hold, to protect, to preserve the Earth.
He tells us that those who work to protect the environment and maintain healthy ecosystems on this planet Earth are allies of this Bodhisattva.
Finally, I have a Dharma name for my companions in this work of so many decades.
And now it's come to this, this virtual sesshin, resonating with so many previous long sits at Red Cedar Dharma Hall, Loon Lake, UBC, and Samish.
How am I sitting here with all of you this Saturday morning?
My introduction to Red Cedar springs directly from dinner one night, during my first day at City Center.
I sat at a table with an older couple who turned out to be Lou and Blanche Hartman, ancestral teachers in our Suzuki Roshi American Zen heritage.
Zenki Blanche asked where I was from, and I said the Skagit Valley.
And she immediately responded, "You should go check out the Bellingham Sangha."

A few days after returning home, I looked up the address, started the car, crossed the Swinomish Channel Bridge, drove across the valley, turned north up I-5, and 45 minutes later, I first sat with this welcoming sangha.
My formal practice began, and I've never looked back.
Endless deep vows.
And now, like an old man, I'm sitting here with you.
Endless deep vows.
And now, like an old horse, my car almost drives to Bellingham by itself.
Reflecting on my practice in preparation for this talk, I'd like to offer a few moments from these past 10 years that have risen from memory as annealing, strengthening, and heartening.

The first work period at Tassajara, entering the woodworking shop and reading on a flitch sawn plank, *the way-seeking mind is actualized by rolling up your sleeves.* Chanting evening refuges, leaving the zendo, Kabarga Creek rumbling, trail-marking kerosene lamps flickering orange, and crisp April air.
Season opening of the Tassajara Gate for the new visitor season, Miyogen Steve Stuckey welcoming all beings with his horsehair hosu.

Writing Wind Cave haiku with Miyogen Steve and Suzuki Roshi's Kaisando, then driving with him back to San Francisco after picking up empty shotgun shells from Lookback Point, [unclear: "last viewed back to Zen Shinji"].
Sitting in City Center Buddha Hall with Zenkei Blanche and Myozenjo Amaral, with thumping mokugyo, chanting endless repetitions of Enmei Jukokunangyo.
Initiating with Bob Penny and Nomon Tim our annual circumambulation of Mount Iri in the Anacortes community forest lands, celebrating first skunk cabbage.

On the May 2016 Japan trip with Mountain Rain, staying at Rinzo Inn, Suzuki Roshi's home monastery, sitting in the corner of the 250-year-old zendo, red lacquered monk's storage boxes along the back wall.
Trimming and cleaning the abbot's memorial stupas with John Wiley.
Walking in the footsteps of Dogen and our ancestors at Eiheiji, waking at 3:30 for early morning service, chanting to the beat of a five-foot-tall mokugyo.
With his grandson's toys scattered about the Buddha Hall, Hoitsu Suzuki, Shunryu's son, presenting a Dharma talk and reminding us to practice with joy.
At Hasadera pilgrimage site, stroking the pearl-smooth, hand-rubbed big toe of the 30-foot-tall Kannon, carved from one massive camphor tree, supposedly in one night.

The hand-hammered Dharma wheel on the ancient cypress pillar behind the Kannon shrine, turned for so many generations, the wood smooth and furrowed an inch deep, the image still the screensaver on this computer.
After the first sesshin as Assistant Tenzo, Rohatsu 2015, Shudo Chris Burkhart warning me, "Don't get trapped by this position."
And ever since, it has been a constant source of joy and liberation.
Practice in action, nourishing the Sangha and all beings.
And my first dokusan with Shinmon Michael Newton, realizing that practice had gifted me a structure to express and act out my profound gratitude.
I'll conclude this ramble with the Tenzo's prayer I offered Nomon Tim when he ascended to his place as our guiding teacher.
*Between cushion and chopping block, no walls, no floor.
Stirring grass soup or cream soup, harmonizing the six flavors, nourishing all beings.
Sharpening knives, wiping bowls, with our kitchen ancestors beyond number, we listen to and accept your teachings to guide us on the way.
I am humbled and honored you have given me this opportunity to share your responsibility, Nomon Tim, to nurture and care for our practice together.
Thank you.
May our intentions extend equally to every being and place with the true merit of the Buddha's way.*
*Beings are numberless.
I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.*
